citation: Zhan M, Tu S, Yang S, Yin Y, Wang Z, Zhang F, et al. Clinical Utility of Metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing in Diagnosing Central Nervous System Infections in Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant Recipients: A Retrospective and Prospective Cohort Study. Infection and Drug Resistance. 2026;19:505-482 (Dove Press, doi:10.2147/IDR.S554425).
study_design: Mixed retrospective and prospective cohort (87 retrospective, 40 prospective), single centre (Peking University People's Hospital)

population.population_description: 127 patients with suspected CNS infection (acute fever >38.5 C plus at least one neurologic sign) undergoing CSF mNGS. Underlying disease: allo-HSCT 70 (55.1%), hematologic malignancies 15 (11.8%), autoimmune disease 11 (8.7%), cerebrovascular disease 5, Guillain-Barre 3, others 7, not applicable elsewhere. N usable by us = 70 allo-HSCT + 15 HM = 85.
population.haemato_subtypes: allo-HSCT 70 (55.1%); hematologic malignancies 15 (11.8%). Pathogens detected in 14/20 positives in allo-HSCT, 3/20 in HM.

index_test.platform_or_panel: In-house CSF mNGS: QIAamp DNA Microbiome Kit extraction, Illumina NextSeq 550Dx, 75-bp single-end, >=20 million reads/sample; Kraken2 taxonomy vs NCBI-derived database; positivity by species-specific RPM ratio (Rr) cutoffs from ROC analysis
index_test.dna_and_or_rna: DNA only (RNA viruses would not be detected; DNA extraction only)

reference_standard: Composite of conventional methods (culture, ink stain, cryptococcal antigen) OR Sanger sequencing (PCR-based orthogonal confirmation of mNGS/PCR findings); positive = any pathogen identified by conventional methods or Sanger sequencing

comparator_2x2.against: Reference criterion: any pathogen identified by conventional methods or Sanger sequencing (reconstructed from reported sensitivity 82.6% = 19/23, specificity 99.0% = 103/104, mNGS-positive n = 20, mNGS-negative n = 107)

diagnostic_yield.basis: mNGS positive in 20/127 (15.7%) CSF samples; conventional methods positive in 4/127 (3.1%); Sanger sequencing positive in 19/127 (15.0%).

additional_yield_vs_conventional: mNGS detected 20 pathogen-positive samples of which 19 were confirmed by Sanger sequencing; conventional methods detected only 4 positives, and all pathogen-positive samples by Sanger or mNGS were negative by conventional methods except the 4 conventional positives. Four mNGS/Sanger-negative cases were culture/CrAg positive (S. lugdunensis, C. minutissimum, R. marceus, one CrAg+).

quality_flags.overlap_risk: Major incorporation bias: 19 of the 23 reference-positive cases were defined by Sanger sequencing confirmation of mNGS findings, so mNGS effectively contributes to its own reference standard. Only 4 reference positives came from conventional methods.

quadas2_notes: 2x2 reconstructed from Table 3 (mNGS positive 20/15.7%, negative 107; sensitivity 82.6%, specificity 99.0%, PPV 95.0%, NPV 96.3%) and is internally consistent. Reference standard heavily dependent on Sanger confirmation of mNGS targets - incorporation/verification bias; patients with negative mNGS and negative conventional tests counted as true negatives without clinical follow-up diagnosis. DNA-only panel (misses RNA viruses). Population is mixed (55% allo-HSCT, 12% HM, remainder non-haemato/neurologic), so haemato-stratified accuracy not available. Authors acknowledge non-random selection and reliance on Sanger for the ROC-positive definition.

evidence_quotes.quote: A total of 127 patients with suspected CNSIs were prospectively enrolled for this study between May 2018 and August 2022.

The specificity and sensitivity of mNGS were 99.0% and 82.6%, respectively (Table 3). Conventional methods and Sanger sequencing both demonstrated a specificity of 100.0%, while their sensitivities were 17.4% and 82.6%, respectively (Table 3). Notably, combining mNGS with conventional methods increased sensitivity to 100.0%, while specificity remained at 99.0%.

To evaluate the diagnostic performance of mNGS for pathogen detection in CSF, we established a reference criterion, defining a positive result as any pathogen identified by conventional methods or Sanger sequencing.
Remarkably, mNGS detected 20 pathogen-positive cases, whereas conventional methods identified only four. Furthermore, 19 of the mNGS-positive cases were confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

Three samples that tested positive by culture for S. lugdunensis, C. minutissimum, and R. marceu, as well as one CrAg-positive sample from a patient with severe CNSI symptoms, were not detected by mNGS (Supplemental Figure 2) or Sanger sequencing.
The distribution of underlying disease varied significantly between the two cohorts (p <0.001), with allo-HSCT being the predominant condition in the retrospective cohort (64.4%)

The suspicion of CNS infections was based on the presence of acute fever (> 38.5°C) accompanied by at least one of the following clinical signs: (1) stiff neck, (2) altered consciousness, (3) increased anterior fontanelle tension, or (4) meningeal irritation.

Library preparation and sequences were performed using the NextSeq 550Dx High Output Reagent Kit v2.5 (Illumina). A 75-bp single-end sequencing was performed and at least 20 million sequencing reads were obtained for each sample.
Pathogens were most frequently detected in patients who had undergone allo-HSCT (14/20), followed by those with underlying hematological malignancies (HM) (3/20)
